E5A01: At resonance, XL and XC cancel each other overall, but each one still carries the full current, so the voltage across each reactance can be Q times the applied voltage.
E5A02: f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)). R doesn't change resonance. 1 / (2 pi sqrt(50 uH x 40 pF)) = 3.56 MHz.
E5A03: Series resonance: XL and XC cancel, leaving only R. So impedance is about equal to the circuit resistance (a minimum).
E5A04: Parallel RLC at resonance: the L and C branches cancel each other, leaving only R. Same answer as for series: about equal to the circuit resistance.
E5A05: Higher Q means a sharper, narrower response, so matching bandwidth decreases.
E5A06: Parallel LC at resonance: energy sloshes back and forth between L and C, so the circulating current is at its maximum.
E5A07: Parallel resonance has maximum impedance, so the current drawn at the input is at its minimum.
E5A08: At resonance the reactances cancel, the circuit looks purely resistive, and voltage and current are in phase.
E5A09: Parallel Q = R / X. Series Q is the flip: X / R.
E5A10: f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)) = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(50 uH x 10 pF)) = 7.12 MHz. R is a decoy.
E5A13: Higher Q in a series resonant circuit means higher internal voltages across L and C (Q times the applied voltage).
E5B01: One time constant (RC) = charging to 63.2%, or discharging to 36.8%.
E5B02: Susceptance = B. (G = conductance, X = reactance, Y = admittance.) Memory hook: suscepta-B-ce.
E5B03: Impedance to admittance in polar form: take 1 / magnitude and flip the sign of the angle.
E5B04: Two 220 uF in parallel = 440 uF. Two 1 Mohm in parallel = 0.5 Mohm. RC = 440 uF x 0.5 Mohm = 220 s.
E5B05: Susceptance is just the reciprocal of reactance: B = 1/X.
E5B06: Susceptance is the imaginary part of admittance (Y = G + jB).
E5B07: Net X = XL - XC = 250 - 500 = -250 (capacitive). Angle = arctan(250/1000) = 14 deg. Capacitive means voltage lags current.
E5B08: Net X = 100 - 300 = -200 (capacitive). Angle = arctan(200/100) = 63 deg. Capacitive means voltage lags current.
E5B09: Capacitor: current leads voltage by 90 deg. Memory hook: ELI the ICE man: in a C, I comes before E.
E5B10: Inductor: voltage leads current by 90 deg. Memory hook: ELI the ICE man: in an L, E comes before I.
E5B11: Net X = 75 - 25 = +50 (inductive). Angle = arctan(50/100) = 27 deg. Inductive means voltage leads current.
E5B12: Admittance is the inverse of impedance: Y = 1/Z.
E5C01: Capacitive reactance is negative j: pure 100 ohms capacitive = 0 - j100.
E5C02: Polar form = magnitude and phase angle. Rectangular form = real and imaginary (R and X).
E5C03: Pure inductive reactance points straight up: +90 deg. Capacitive is -90 deg.
E5C04: Frequency response graphs usually use a logarithmic scale (dB).
E5C05: A phasor diagram shows the phase relationships between impedances at one frequency.
E5C06: 50 - j25: 50 ohms resistance, and the minus j means 25 ohms of capacitive reactance.
E5C07: Pure resistance has no reactance, so it sits on the horizontal (R) axis.
E5C08: Phase angles are shown in polar coordinates (magnitude and angle).
E5C09: Rectangular impedance plot: X axis = resistance, Y axis = reactance (+ inductive, - capacitive).
E5C10: XC = 1 / (2 pi x 14 MHz x 38 pF), about 300 ohms. So 400 - j300: right 400, down 300, which is point 4.
E5C11: XL = 2 pi x 3.505 MHz x 18 uH, about 400 ohms. So 300 + j400: right 300, up 400, which is point 3.
E5C12: XC = 1 / (2 pi x 21.2 MHz x 19 pF), about 400 ohms. So 300 - j400: right 300, down 400, which is point 1.
E5D01: Skin effect: at RF, current crowds to the conductor's surface, so resistance rises with frequency.
E5D02: At VHF and up, every lead is an inductor. Keep leads short to minimize inductive reactance.
E5D03: Reactive power means voltage and current are 90 degrees out of phase.
E5D04: At microwaves, even short wires are a meaningful fraction of a wavelength. Keep connections short to limit phase shift.
E5D05: Electrolytic capacitors have too much internal inductance to work at RF.
E5D06: An inductor's self-resonance comes from the capacitance between its turns.
E5D07: Self-resonance = the component's nominal reactance plus its parasitic reactance (L with stray C, or C with stray L).
E5D08: Film capacitors at RF lose mostly to skin effect in their thin metal films.
E5D09: Ideal L and C store energy in fields and give it back. No power is dissipated.
E5D10: A thicker conductor is electrically longer. That's why thick dipoles get cut a bit shorter.
E5D11: Only the resistor burns real power: P = I^2 x R = 1^2 x 100 = 100 W. The reactance consumes nothing.
E5D12: Reactive power is wattless: it goes back and forth and does no work.
E6A01: Gallium arsenide is for microwave circuits (high electron mobility, see E6E01).
E6A02: N-type = extra free electrons (Negative). P-type = extra holes (Positive).
E6A03: Reverse bias pulls holes and electrons away from the junction, widening the depletion region, so no current flows.
E6A04: An acceptor impurity accepts electrons, which leaves holes (P-type). A donor donates electrons (N-type).
E6A05: A FET gate is insulated or reverse-biased, so a FET has much higher input impedance than a bipolar transistor.
E6A06: Beta = current gain: the change in collector current divided by the change in base current.
E6A07: A silicon junction turns on at about 0.6-0.7 V base to emitter.
E6A08: Alpha cutoff: the grounded-base current gain (alpha) falls to 0.7 of its low-frequency value.
E6A09: A depletion-mode FET is normally ON: current flows with zero gate voltage, and you apply gate voltage to turn it off.
E6A10: Look for two gates (G1, G2) and the arrow pointing in (N-channel), which is symbol 4. Memory hook: N = arrow iN.
E6A11: A JFET has the gate connected straight to the channel. Arrow pointing out = P-channel, which is symbol 1. Memory hook: P = Pointing out.
E6A12: Zeners across a MOSFET gate protect the thin gate insulation from static damage.
E6B01: A Zener diode holds a constant voltage while the current through it varies. It's a voltage reference.
E6B02: Schottky diodes have a lower forward voltage drop (about 0.3 V), so they waste less power as rectifiers.
E6B03: An LED's forward voltage is set by the material's band gap, which also sets its color.
E6B04: A varactor diode is a voltage-controlled capacitor (vari-able cap-acitor).
E6B05: PIN diodes switch RF because of their low junction capacitance when off.
E6B06: Schottky diodes are fast, so they're common as VHF/UHF mixers and detectors.
E6B07: Too much current kills a diode by overheating the junction.
E6B08: A Schottky diode is a metal-semiconductor junction.
E6B09: Point-contact diodes are classic RF detectors (the old crystal radio cat's whisker).
E6B10: The Schottky symbol has an S-shaped cathode bar, with hooks at both ends. That's symbol 6.
E6B11: A PIN diode's RF attenuation is controlled by its forward DC bias current.
E6C01: Hysteresis gives a comparator two thresholds, so noise around the switching point can't make the output chatter.
E6C02: When the input crosses the threshold, the comparator's output changes state. That's its whole job.
E6C03: Tri-state = 0, 1, and high-impedance (disconnected), so many devices can share a bus.
E6C04: BiCMOS combines the high input impedance of CMOS with the low output impedance (strong drive) of bipolar transistors.
E6C05: CMOS has the lowest power consumption: it draws almost nothing when it isn't switching.
E6C06: CMOS switches at about half the supply voltage, which leaves a wide noise margin on both sides.
E6C07: A pull-up or pull-down resistor sets a known voltage on an input or output that would otherwise float open.
E6C08: NAND = AND shape (flat back, round front) plus a bubble at the output. That's symbol 2.
E6C09: FPGAs are configured with a hardware description language (HDL), such as VHDL or Verilog.
E6C10: NOR = OR shape (curved back, pointed front) plus a bubble at the output. That's symbol 4.
E6C11: NOT (inverter) = a triangle with a bubble at the output. That's symbol 5.
E6D01: Piezoelectricity works both ways: squeeze the material and it makes a voltage; apply a voltage and it flexes.
E6D02: A crystal's equivalent circuit is a series RLC (the motional arm) in parallel with a shunt C (the electrodes and holder).
E6D03: Piezoelectric effect: a voltage causes mechanical deformation. A magnetic field doesn't (that's magnetostriction).
E6D04: Laminated (thin-layer) cores break up eddy currents, which reduces core loss.
E6D05: Ferrite has higher permeability than powdered iron, so it needs fewer turns for the same inductance.
E6D06: A core's permeability determines the inductance. Permittivity is for capacitors.
E6D08: Powdered iron is the most temperature-stable core material, which is why it's used in stable tuned circuits.
E6D09: Ferrite beads on an amplifier's leads suppress VHF/UHF parasitic oscillations.
E6D10: A toroid keeps most of its magnetic field inside the core, so it couples less to nearby parts.
E6D11: Brass (a nonmagnetic conductor) lowers inductance: eddy currents in it push the field out. Ferrite raises it.
E6D12: Saturation = too much magnetic flux: the core can't magnetize any further.
E6E01: GaAs has higher electron mobility, so it's faster at UHF and microwave.
E6E02: DIP (dual in-line package) is through-hole. PLCC, BGA, and SOT are surface mount.
E6E03: Gallium nitride (GaN) supports the highest frequency in MMICs.
E6E04: MMICs are usually 50 ohms in and out.
E6E05: A good UHF low-noise preamp has a noise figure around 0.5 dB.
E6E06: MMICs are popular for their controlled gain, low noise figure, and constant 50-ohm input and output impedances across their range.
E6E07: MMICs connect through microstrip, a trace over a ground plane on the circuit board.
E6E08: Most MMICs get their power through a resistor and/or RF choke on the output lead.
E6E09: Surface-mount parts have no leads, so they have the least parasitic effects above HF.
E6E10: All of these are SMT advantages: smaller area, shorter traces, less parasitic L and C.
E6E11: DIP = dual in-line package: two rows of pins on opposite sides.
E6E12: DIP leads are too long for UHF: they add parasitic inductance.
E6F01: In a photovoltaic cell, electrons absorb the light's energy and break free to become current.
E6F02: Light frees charge carriers in photoconductive material, so its resistance decreases.
E6F03: An optoisolator = an LED shining on a phototransistor.
E6F04: Photovoltaic effect = light converted directly into electrical energy.
E6F05: An optical shaft encoder senses rotation with a patterned wheel that interrupts a light beam.
E6F06: Photoconductive devices are made from crystalline semiconductor.
E6F07: A solid-state relay does a relay's job with semiconductors: no moving parts.
E6F08: Optoisolators give electrical isolation between the low-voltage control side and the 120 VAC side.
E6F09: Photovoltaic efficiency = the fraction of light energy converted to electrical output.
E6F11: A fully lit silicon cell puts out about 0.5 V open circuit.
